enrichment.short_title: Letter of credit escrow entitlement after Tomlin order

statutes_considered.title: ICC Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1993 Revision)

key_facts: Sirius fronted a Lloyd's reinsurance for Agnew with FAI as retrocessionaire and obtained a US$5m Westpac letter of credit.
A 3 September 1999 agreement restricted Sirius from drawing the letter of credit unless FAI agreed Sirius should pay Agnew or Agnew obtained judgment or arbitration award against Sirius.
After FAI entered provisional liquidation, a Tomlin order compromised arbitration, drew down the letter of credit into escrow, and acknowledged FAI's US$22.5m debt to Sirius.
Jacob J held Sirius entitled to the escrow proceeds; the Court of Appeal allowed FAI's appeal on Tomlin construction and dismissed Sirius's cross-appeal on letter-of-credit autonomy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court trial of preliminary issues on entitlement to escrow proceeds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; FAI entitled to the letter of credit proceeds in escrow; cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties expressly agree contractual restrictions on drawing a letter of credit, the beneficiary is not entitled as against the applicant to realise the credit if those conditions are unfulfilled, even though the credit remains autonomous as between beneficiary and bank; an express negative covenant may be enforced by injunction.
legal_issues: Construction of paragraph 1 of the Tomlin order schedule
Whether Tomlin paragraphs 4 and 5 preserved letter-of-credit arguments
Autonomy of letters of credit versus underlying contractual draw-down conditions
Whether Sirius could draw the letter of credit in breach of the September 1999 agreement

enrichment.short_title: Housing association's right to possession after council notice to quit
key_facts: Islington Council leased temporary housing to Alamo Housing Co-Operative, which sublet to seven occupiers without security of tenure.
Clause 2(1) of the lease contained an exception allowing Alamo to retain possession after the council's notice to quit solely for the purpose of enabling eviction if required.
After the council's notice expired, Alamo served notices to quit on subtenants and brought CPR Part 55 possession claims.
Subtenants argued Alamo lacked sufficient interest to bring possession proceedings once the council's notice had taken effect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a district judge's possession orders, with permission granted after reallocation to the multi-track.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; Alamo held to have continuing right to possession for eviction purposes.
enrichment.ratio: Where a council's notice to quit has expired but the lease expressly preserves the tenant's right to possession for the purpose of evicting subtenants, that exception confers sufficient title to bring possession proceedings against occupiers who have no independent right to remain.
legal_issues: Interest required to bring possession proceedings under CPR Part 55
Construction of the exception in clause 2(1) of the head lease
Whether a licensee without an estate can obtain possession against trespassers or subtenants
Distinction between Manchester Airport v Dutton and Countryside Residential v A Child

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of CPS refusal to prosecute care-home drowning

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 1995

key_facts: Malcolm Rowley, a severely disabled 30-year-old in Salford Council care, drowned in a bath after being left unsupervised by carers Sarah Peters and Brenda Mather in July 1998.
Repeated police and CPS reviews concluded insufficient evidence for gross negligence manslaughter against carers or the council.

Mrs Rowley sought judicial review of Mr Enzor's February 2002 CPS decision after extensive investigations, an inquest finding accidental death with contributory neglect, and HSE prosecution of the council.
The court held subjective recklessness was relevant but not determinative in assessing gross negligence, and corporate manslaughter required an identified directing mind.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Crown Prosecution Service's decision not to prosecute for gross negligence manslaughter.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; CPS decision upheld as lawful and within discretion.
enrichment.ratio: In gross negligence manslaughter the Adomako test is objective, but a prosecutor or jury may take the defendant's state of mind into account when assessing whether conduct was so bad as to be criminal; absence of subjective recklessness does not preclude prosecution, but mitigating factors including lack of awareness of risk may weigh against criminality.
legal_issues: Legal test for gross negligence manslaughter after R v Adomako
Relevance of subjective recklessness to grossness and criminality
Corporate manslaughter and identification of a directing mind
Article 2 ECHR procedural duty and CPS investigatory role
Evidential test in Code for Crown Prosecutors

enrichment.short_title: VAT refund for converting part-residential pub to dwelling
key_facts: Lady Blom-Cooper converted a former public house at 1 Southgate Road, London, into a single family dwelling.
The first and second floors had previously been residential; ground floor, cellar and roof space were non-residential.
The VAT tribunal allowed a section 35 refund for works converting the non-residential parts; the High Court dismissed the Commissioners' appeal.
The Court of Appeal held Note (9) to Group 5 of Schedule 8 applied via section 35(4), denying relief because no additional dwelling was created.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court decision on a VAT and Duties Tribunal appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; VAT refund claim rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Section 35(4) VATA 1994 requires Note (9) to Group 5 of Schedule 8 to apply when construing section 35(1D); where a building already contains a residential part, conversion of a non-residential part qualifies as a residential conversion only if an additional dwelling is created.
legal_issues: Meaning of residential conversion under section 35(1D) VATA 1994
Application of Note (9) to Group 5 Schedule 8 to DIY builder refunds
Whether partial conversion of mixed-use building qualifies for section 35 relief
Parallel construction of zero-rating items 1(b) and 3 of Group 5

enrichment.short_title: Lawfulness of police cordon over public right of way
key_facts: After a stabbing in Edmonton Green shopping centre, police cordoned off areas of a mall over which a public right of way existed.
Mr Morrison challenged the cordon, was arrested for disorderly conduct and alleged wilful obstruction of PC Sandell.
Wood Green Crown Court held the cordon unlawful, found no case to answer, and acquitted Morrison on both charges.
The Divisional Court held police may assume owner consent to preserve a crime scene and that the cordon was lawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case stated appeal to the Divisional Court from Wood Green Crown Court's no-case-to-answer ruling.
enrichment.outcome: Both questions answered in the affirmative; Crown Court held wrong in law; no remittal sought.
enrichment.ratio: Police officers preserving the scene of a serious crime on private land subject to a public right of way may lawfully erect a temporary cordon by assuming the owner's consent and exercising a common law power to do what is necessary and reasonable to preserve evidence, provided they do not exceed what is reasonable.
legal_issues: Common law power to cordon off crime scenes on private land with public rights of way
Whether Terrorism Act 2000 is the only statutory cordon power
Lawfulness of arrest and obstruction where cordon is unlawful
Section 5 Public Order Act 1986: likelihood versus proof of harassment alarm or distress
Proper content of a case stated

confidence.notes: Important public law ruling on police crime-scene powers; case stated criticised but legal conclusions clear.

enrichment.short_title: Inland Revenue informer denied discretionary reward
key_facts: Mr Churchhouse supplied information to the Inland Revenue about a corporate taxpayer's tax affairs and sought a reward.
He had previously received rewards of £1,200 and £6,265 in 2000 for other information.
The Revenue refused payment, finding the information either duplicated existing knowledge or related to historic periods it could not review.
Churchhouse challenged the refusal by judicial review, arguing a mandatory entitlement and unlawful policy tests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of refusal to pay an informer's reward.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no arguable ground to challenge exercise of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Section 32 of the Inland Revenue Regulation Act 1890 confers a discretion, not a duty, to pay rewards; the Revenue may adopt a reasonable policy requiring tax recovery to result from information provided, and a disappointed informer cannot demand disclosure of taxpayer-confidential reasons for refusal.
legal_issues: Whether section 32 IRRA 1890 creates a mandatory or discretionary reward
Lawfulness of 'leads to recovery' policy for informer rewards
Legitimate expectation of reward
Wednesbury challenge to Revenue decision
Confidentiality constraints on judicial review of tax informer claims

enrichment.short_title: Driving home after fatal accident not perverting justice
key_facts: Mark Clark hit and killed a cyclist on the A38 after drinking heavily, drove home with a damaged car, and reported the incident the next morning.
He was convicted of doing an act tending and intended to pervert the course of justice for leaving the scene to avoid breathalyser evidence.
The Crown relied on removing himself and his damaged car from the scene; it did not rely on failure to stop or report as the actus reus.
The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction, holding driving home without more did not conceal evidence tending to pervert justice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction, with leave granted on whether facts could constitute the offence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed; defendant's costs order made.
enrichment.ratio: Perverting the course of justice requires a positive act or course of conduct tending to pervert justice; simply driving home after a fatal accident while over the limit, without more, does not conceal blood-alcohol evidence or vehicle damage so as to constitute the offence, even where intent is established.
legal_issues: Scope of common law offence of perverting the course of justice
Whether driving away from accident scene conceals evidence
Requirement of positive act versus omission after R v Headley
Relationship with section 170 Road Traffic Act 1988 duties
Article 7 ECHR certainty and incremental extension of common law crimes

confidence.notes: Clear CA criminal judgment limiting offence ambit; alternative RTA charges noted.

enrichment.short_title: BBC wildlife cameramen not workers for union recognition

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: BECTU sought statutory trade union recognition for freelance wildlife cameramen and women working for the BBC Natural History Unit.
The Central Arbitration Committee held they were workers under section 296(1)(b) because they were not professionals exercising activity regulated by a professional body.
The BBC challenged the decision by judicial review, arguing the cameramen were professionals or operated as independent businesses.
Moses J quashed the decision, holding the CAC erred in law by treating regulation by a professional body as an essential requirement of professional status.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review hearing with urgency of BECTU recognition application against CAC decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; CAC decision quashed; matter remitted to a different panel.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation by a professional body is a relevant but not essential factor in determining whether individuals are professionals for section 296(1)(b); the CAC erred in law by imposing a mandatory regulatory-body test when deciding if freelance cameramen were workers eligible for collective bargaining recognition.
legal_issues: Meaning of professional client exception in section 296(1)(b)
Whether wildlife cameramen are workers or professionals
Standard of judicial review of Central Arbitration Committee decisions
Group versus individual assessment of worker status
Whether contacts list members seek to work under section 296(1)

enrichment.short_title: Seven-year children policy applies to port asylum cases
key_facts: A Roma mother and two sons from Poland claimed asylum on second entry in December 1999 after an earlier failed claim and return in 1999.
They sought exceptional leave relying on DP 5/96 modified by the seven-year concession for families with children continuously resident seven or more years.
The Home Office refused, treating the policy as applying only to enforcement/removal cases and finding residence continuity broken by the three-month return to Poland.
The Court of Appeal held the policy applies to port cases and that on the facts continuity was broken, so no presumption in favour of leave arose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review in the Court of Appeal after grant of permission to apply for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; refusal of exceptional leave upheld.
enrichment.ratio: The Home Secretary's seven-year children concession (DP 5/96 as modified) applies by analogy to port refusal cases as well as deportation and removal cases, but a family whose continuous residence was broken by voluntary return home after a failed asylum claim does not qualify for the policy presumption.
legal_issues: Whether DP 5/96 seven-year concession applies to port entry cases
Continuity of residence where family returned to country of origin
Construction of ministerial immigration policy concessions
Article 8 ECHR and exceptional leave decisions

confidence.notes: Important policy-scope ruling conceded at hearing; outcome turns on fact-specific continuity assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Care fact-finding halted prematurely in abuse case
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned alleged sexual abuse of stepdaughter T by stepfather AK, supported by paediatric findings of traumatic genital injury on two examinations.
Dr San Lazaro's evidence was excluded after criticism in Lilley and Reed v Newcastle City Council; Dr Evans and Dr Sunderland ultimately agreed on traumatic injury.
The judge terminated the split fact-finding hearing at the close of the prosecution/local authority case, rejecting medical and disclosure evidence.
The Court of Appeal held the judge wrongly rejected agreed expert evidence and disclosure, and clarified parents are compellable witnesses in care proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against termination of a split care proceedings fact-finding hearing before parents gave evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted for retrial before a different judge.
enrichment.ratio: A judge at a preliminary fact-finding hearing in care proceedings cannot properly halt the inquiry before hearing all evidence where agreed paediatric experts opine traumatic injury occurred and child disclosure evidence has not been adequately assessed; parents are compellable witnesses under section 98 Children Act 1989.
legal_issues: When a judge may terminate a split fact-finding hearing in care proceedings
Admissibility and weight of agreed expert medical evidence
Assessment of child disclosure evidence
Whether parents are compellable witnesses in care proceedings
Effect of Lilley and Reed on reliance on Dr San Lazaro
